opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea in that work is that norms aren't just rules sitting in some agent's head. They're shared expectations, and what makes them work is that everyone holds beliefs about what everyone else is going to do and about what everyone else thinks is appropriate.

In the Markov-game setting, we model agents who start out uncertain about which norms are in force. They might have some prior over possible norm systems, things like "you shouldn't harvest apples from someone else's territory" or "you should contribute to cleaning the river." They're watching other agents act and asking: given what I'm seeing, which norms are these agents probably following? That's a Bayesian inverse-planning problem. You assume others are roughly rational and also responsive to norms, and you invert their behavior to infer the norms that best explain it.

The beliefs about others' behavior do a lot of work here. First, they make learning much more sample-efficient. You don't have to discover a norm by getting punished for breaking it many times. You can watch a few people avoid an action they'd clearly benefit from, and infer there's probably a rule against it. Humans do this all the time. A kid notices nobody cuts in line and picks up the norm without anyone stating it.

Second, those beliefs are what make coordination possible. A norm only helps if I can rely on you following it too. If I believe you'll respect property boundaries, I can invest in my own patch without worrying it gets stripped. So the belief that others comply is part of what makes complying worthwhile. It's self-reinforcing: shared beliefs support shared behavior, which supports the beliefs.

What we found interesting is that this lets agents converge on a shared normative understanding fairly quickly, even when they start with different guesses, and it lets newcomers join an established society and pick up its norms just by observing. That matters for AI, because we don't want systems that only learn to cooperate through endless trial and error with fixed partners. We want systems that can walk into a human social context, notice the unwritten rules, and adapt the way a thoughtful newcomer would.

It also connects to a broader view I hold about alignment: a lot of what we care about isn't a fixed reward function but a structured, socially shared set of norms and contracts. Modeling how agents form beliefs about those norms, and about each other, seems to me a more faithful picture of how cooperation actually works than treating everything as individual utility maximization.

r001.rationale: The response says shared beliefs make coordination possible and that agents can converge on shared norms, but it does not connect initial behavior beliefs to selecting better equilibria in the extended Markov game.

r002.rationale: It describes agents as rational and norm-responsive, but does not clearly state that they pursue individual objectives subject to rules they believe most of society follows.

r003.rationale: It describes Bayesian inference from observed actions, including inferring a rule when others avoid an action that would benefit them, and says agents infer norms that best explain the behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Right, so the way I think about it is that beliefs about other agents' behavior are really doing the heavy lifting for both learning and coordination, and they're doing it in a way that's a bit different from how people usually set up multi-agent reinforcement learning.

In the standard Markov game setup, you've got a bunch of agents, each with their own reward function, and the typical thing is to just have everyone optimize and hope you land in some equilibrium. But if you look at how humans actually deal with norms, that's not really what's going on. When I walk into a new country and I'm trying to figure out which side of the escalator to stand on, I'm not solving a game-theoretic problem from scratch. I'm watching what other people do, I'm forming beliefs about what they expect of me, and I'm inferring that there's a rule here, even though nobody's told me what it is.

So in our framework, the key move is that agents maintain beliefs about what norms are in place, and those beliefs are learned by observing the behavior of others. We treat norms as something like constraints or obligations that modify what agents are willing to do, and then each agent is doing Bayesian inference over which norms are operative, given the behavior they see. If I see everyone consistently avoiding a certain action, even when it would be individually beneficial for them, that's evidence there's a prohibition in place. If I see people consistently going out of their way to do something costly, that's evidence of an obligation.

What this gives you is that beliefs about other agents' behavior become the bridge between individual learning and collective coordination. Because if I believe other agents are norm-following, and I believe a particular norm is in place, then I can predict what they're going to do, and I can choose my own behavior to be compatible with that. And crucially, if I also follow the norm myself, I'm generating more evidence for everyone else, which stabilizes the whole thing. You get this nice self-reinforcing dynamic where the norm becomes common knowledge not because anyone announced it, but because everyone's beliefs converge through observation.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this handles the case where agents join a population midway through. In a lot of multi-agent learning setups, if you add a new agent, you've got to retrain everything. But in our framework, a new agent can just observe the existing population for a while, infer the norms, and then start complying. That's much closer to how human socialization works, and I think it's important for AI systems that are going to be deployed into existing human social contexts rather than trained from scratch alongside everyone they'll interact with.

And honestly, part of my motivation here is about alignment more broadly. There's a tendency to frame alignment as, we need to get the right reward function or the right preferences into the system. But a lot of what makes human cooperation work isn't that we all share the same preferences. It's that we have shared norms that we can infer and comply with even when our individual goals differ. So building agents that can learn norms from observing others, and that reason about others as norm-following agents too, seems like a more realistic foundation than trying to specify everything up front.

r001.rationale: The response says beliefs help agents predict and coordinate compatible behavior, but does not explain how initial beliefs help them reach better equilibria in the extended Markov game.

r002.rationale: It describes agents with differing individual goals treating inferred norms as constraints and complying with norms they believe are in place across the population.

r003.rationale: It explains that agents infer norms from observed behavior, including treating costly actions or avoiding individually beneficial actions as evidence of obligations or prohibitions.

astra-6.text:
I think beliefs are central because whether it makes sense to follow a norm often depends on what you expect other people to do. In a Markov game, the consequences of your actions depend on the other agents’ actions as well. So you’re learning how to act in an environment where the other agents are also learning and adapting.

Take a simple coordination problem, like choosing which side of a path to walk on. Neither side is inherently better, but having a shared expectation makes everyone’s behavior more predictable. If I expect you to keep left, that gives me a reason to keep left too. And as we repeatedly interact, those expectations can become mutually reinforcing.

But I would distinguish expecting a behavior from thinking that behavior is a norm. An agent might predict that others will do something without believing that they ought to do it. To capture that distinction, we need to consider expectations about approval, correction, or sanctions, and how those enter the agents’ decisions.

So beliefs help explain both how coordination becomes possible and why a norm persists. They also help explain why changing a norm can be difficult: even if everyone would prefer a different arrangement, each agent may continue following the existing convention because they expect everyone else to keep following it.

r001.rationale: The response says expectations can support coordination and reinforce a convention, but it does not explain that initial beliefs help agents coordinate on better equilibria in an extended Markov game.

r002.rationale: The response discusses following conventions and social expectations, but does not describe agents pursuing individual objectives while complying with rules they believe most of society follows.

r003.rationale: The response distinguishes predicting behavior from viewing it as a norm, but does not describe agents updating beliefs toward rules that explain others’ behavior better than immediate self-interest alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key idea is that a social norm isn’t just a rule that an agent follows in isolation. It also depends on what the agent expects other people to do, and how it expects them to respond to its own behavior.

In a Markov game, your actions and the actions of other agents jointly determine what happens next. So learning how to act requires some model of those other agents. If I expect you to cooperate, cooperation might make sense for me. But if I expect you to exploit that cooperation, or to ignore a convention we’re trying to establish, I might behave differently.

Those beliefs can support a norm by making everyone’s behavior mutually reinforcing. For example, a convention about yielding only works if we have sufficiently compatible expectations about who will yield. And expectations about whether others will object to a violation can also affect whether an agent follows the norm.

But that creates a learning challenge: agents are learning about one another while also changing their own behavior. So we need to understand not just whether a particular pattern of behavior is stable once everyone expects it, but how agents arrive at those shared expectations—and whether they can revise them when circumstances change.

r001.rationale: The response says compatible expectations can make behavior mutually reinforcing, but does not explain how initial beliefs help agents coordinate on better equilibria in the extended Markov game.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents following conventions and considering others’ responses, but does not describe pursuing individual objectives subject to rules believed to be followed by most of society.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning about other agents and revising expectations, but not updating beliefs toward rules that explain others’ behavior better than immediate self-interest alone.
